..
Issued at 119 AM EST Mon Nov 23 2026

Colder air continues to steadily press into northern MI, on nw 
winds. Some initial post-frontal drizzle has turned considerably 
more showery, in part due to increasing instability over the 
unseasonably warm Great Lakes. Several upticks and downticks in 
coverage/intensity are expected over the next 36 hours. And, as
we get colder, our current rain showers will mix with and turn 
to snow. 

850mb temps lower to -6 to -8C by 12Z, coldest north. Those values 
fall to -8 to -12C by late afternoon, as cold advection persists on 
nw low-level winds. That is counter-balanced by lake water 
temps of +8C on eastern Superior, and +11C on northern Lake MI. 
So, instability is impressive, and a ton of energy and heat 
will be transferred from lake to air. But how cold can near- 
surface air temps get in this scenario? Think it will be a bit 
more of a struggle to lower surface temps than guidance thinks, 
which will result in lower snow-to-liquid ratios. Diurnal 
heating will also be factor in this thinking later today. Lower
teens for SLRs will be most common this afternoon, mid teens 
this evening. As for p-type timing, ongoing precip in western 
Chip/Mack Cos should already be turning, and that process gets 
underway in the higher terrain of northern lower in 2-3 hours. 

A secondary cold front, with some lake aggregate troffing 
characteristics, is making southward progress into upper MI. This 
will bring a band of showers into far northern and north-central 
lower MI before dawn, before this boundary becomes more diffuse. And 
this arrives just as we are getting cold enough to turn over to 
snow. A quick coating of slushy snow (less than an inch) is possible 
early this morning, over the hillier parts of the tip of the mitt 
counties, but especially south of M-68 down into Otsego Co. Coastal 
areas will stay rainier.

This all washes out shortly after 12Z, with just sct lake effect 
showers in both peninsulas for the rest of the morning. But this 
afternoon and very early evening, a sharp shortwave trof digs from 
Lk Superior across northern MI. This rapidly, though briefly, 
increases synoptic-scale forcing/moisture, and pushes inversion 
heights higher. This also resharpens the previously diffuse boundary 
in the south, before shoving it further south. Some potential for a 
surface wave to develop along this boundary, before pushing into nw 
lower MI. Expect a considerable uptick in lake effect snow this 
afternoon, again especially in nw lower. This while our fetch 
is nw veering nnw. QPF max is placed along the southern Kalkaska/
Gd Trav Co border, up to 0.25" liquid 18Z-00Z. Snow amounts here
max out at around 3" near South Boardman. An advisory was 
considered for this small area; this will fall in a reasonably 
short window, with briefly intense snowfall. But I'm not feeling
it at this moment, for an ultimately marginal forecast snow 
accum. No headlines yet.

Nw-nnw flow lake effect snow continues tonight, probably more so 
than guidance thinks. But post-shortwave mid-level subsidence/drying 
and lowering inversion heights will significantly decrease coverage/
intensity. High pressure will build east across lower MI Tuesday,
and lake effect precip will more completely diminish. Still cold.
Even as the surface high departs, surface ridging extends back to
northern MI Tue night/Wednesday, even as systems evolve in the 
central plains and lower MS Valley. So fairly quiet but chilly 
here for that busy travel day.

The disposition of those upstream systems for the end of the week 
remains problematic. A vigorous and negatively tilted southern 
stream shortwave will cause substantial cyclogenesis over and off 
the se US coast, beginning Wednesday. The degree to which this 
interacts with a leftover upper low over the northern plains/upper 
MS Valley is the big question. Earlier thinking that this upper low 
would drift over us while weakening, is looking less and less 
likely. Recent operational ECMWF and GFS runs have more interactions 
between these systems, resulting in an upper low that deepens and 
digs into the lower OH Valley on Thanksgiving, before gradually 
ejecting toward PA/NY, and while more fully absorbing that 
initial southern stream shortwave. And that translates to a most
likely surface low path from the Carolina coast, north to the 
lower lakes. And /that/ would wrap some precip back into 
northern MI, Thu night-Friday in particular. For now this looks
like a rain/snow mix, with rain more likely near the coasts. 
Hard to get too specific with forecast challenges after this, as
the speed of this systems departure remains uncertain. The grids
have spotty chancy pops for the rest of the forecast, with 
seasonably cool temps.
